body:
Meaning and cultural significance

The rural landscape of Gujarat, particularly Kutch and Saurashtra, contains numerous upright stone memorials known as Paliyas or Palias. These stones preserve the memory of individuals whose deaths, sacrifices or lives acquired special significance within their families and communities.

A Paliya is a traditional commemorative stone erected in memory of a deceased person. It may contain carved figures, symbolic motifs and inscriptions identifying the person or circumstances being commemorated.

Many Paliyas commemorate warriors who died in battle, people remembered for protecting villages or cattle, and deceased ancestors. Other memorial stones commemorate women associated with the historical practice of sati.

Paliyas are important examples of Gujarat's cultural heritage because they preserve both physical evidence of the past and community memories transmitted through generations. Some continue to receive offerings and are revered as ancestral memorials.

Major categories of memorial stones

CategoryPerson commemoratedCommon identifying feature
Hero stoneA deceased warrior or community heroMounted warrior or heroic figure
Sati stoneA woman associated with the historical practice of satiRaised hand or arm with bangles
Surdhan ni KhambhiA person who died an unnatural deathMounted warrior; inscription may include Surdhan

Hero stones are also associated with the tradition of Surapara or Suro-Puro, in which a deceased hero or brave ancestor is revered by descendants. The terminology and classification of memorial stones may vary between regions.

Typical structure and symbolism

Many traditional Paliyas have 3 horizontal sections or registers. Each section serves a different commemorative purpose.

  • Upper register: Often contains the Sun, Moon and floral motifs. The celestial symbols are commonly associated with enduring remembrance.
  • Central register: Contains the principal commemorative image. A mounted warrior frequently identifies a hero stone, while a raised arm with bangles commonly identifies a sati memorial.
  • Lower register: May contain an inscription recording the name, date, place or circumstances associated with the deceased. Dates may be expressed in Vikram Samvat.

The figures are frequently carved in relief, meaning that the design projects from the surface of the stone rather than forming a completely free-standing sculpture. Although the 3-register arrangement is common, not every Paliya contains all these features.

Historical evidence and living heritage

Paliyas provide information about local history, clothing, social groups, religious beliefs, commemorative customs and historical events. Their inscriptions are particularly valuable when they preserve identifiable names and dates.

However, inscriptions may be absent, damaged or difficult to interpret. Historians therefore compare physical evidence with other records and oral traditions. An oral account preserves cultural memory, but its historical details may require independent confirmation.

The stone itself belongs to tangible cultural heritage, while the associated oral narratives, commemorative customs and traditional beliefs belong to intangible cultural heritage.

A Paliya is not necessarily a grave or burial marker. Its primary purpose is commemoration. Similarly, not every Paliya commemorates a warrior, and not every Paliya carries an inscription.

Prelims focus

  • Paliyas are traditional memorial stones.
  • Kutch and Saurashtra are particularly associated with this tradition.
  • A mounted warrior commonly represents a hero memorial.
  • A raised arm with bangles commonly represents a sati memorial.
  • Inscriptions may record dates in Vikram Samvat.
  • Trap: Paliyas are not exclusively warrior memorials or burial monuments.

[Sources: Durga Kale, Speaking Stones: Oral Tradition as Provenance for the Memorial Stelae in Gujarat, Heritage, Vol. 2, 2019, pp. 1085–1096, Sections 1, 3 and 4; Ira Bhatnagar and Sushmita Sen, Documentation and Classification of the Paaliyas of Jhalod, Gujarat, Heritage: Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies in Archaeology, 2024; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, chapter Stone, p. 27. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Paliyas: Gujarat's Traditional Memorial Stones

body:
Distribution of traditional memorial stones

Paliyas occur in different parts of Gujarat. They are especially prominent in Kutch and Saurashtra, where historical warfare, pastoral traditions and community remembrance contributed to the establishment of numerous memorials. Similar commemorative traditions are also found in eastern Gujarat.

Bhuchar Mori: Memorial of the battle of 1591

Bhuchar Mori is a historical battlefield near Dhrol in Jamnagar district. A major battle took place here in 1591 between the forces of Nawanagar and the Mughal army during the reign of Emperor Akbar.

Jam Sataji, the ruler of Nawanagar, had refused to surrender the fugitive Muzaffar Shah III, the last Sultan of Gujarat, to the Mughals. The resulting conflict is remembered for the death of several warriors, including Jam Sataji's heir, Prince Ajoji, also written as Ajaji.

The memorial stones at Bhuchar Mori preserve the memory of the battle. The site is an important example of the relationship between historical events, physical memorials and regional folklore.

Jhalod: Memorial traditions of eastern Gujarat

Jhalod taluka in Dahod district contains memorial stones locally known as Sheera. These stones are associated with communities including the Bhil, Baria and Vasava.

The memorials include hero stones, sati stones and pillars commemorating people who died unnatural deaths, known as Surdhan ni Khambhi. Their presence demonstrates that Gujarat's commemorative stone tradition is not restricted to Kutch, Saurashtra or royal families.

Thangadh and Kanmer

Traditional memorial stones are also found at Thangadh in Surendranagar district and Kanmer in Kutch. At some sites, memorial stones associated with royal families are sheltered beneath commemorative structures called Chhatris.

A Chhatri is a canopy-like architectural structure that may serve a commemorative function. A Paliya, by contrast, is the memorial stone itself.

Hamirji Gohil and Somnath

Veer Hamirji Gohil is remembered in Gujarat's historical and oral traditions for sacrificing his life in the defence of Somnath Temple. He is associated with Lathi in Saurashtra. Vegadaji Bhil is also remembered in traditions concerning the defence of Somnath.

A memorial statue of Hamirji Gohil stands near the entrance of Somnath Temple in Gir Somnath district. His story is preserved through regional literature, oral narratives and physical commemoration.

Place and association

PlaceDistrictAssociation
Bhuchar Mori, DhrolJamnagarBattle of 1591 and Prince Ajoji
JhalodDahodSheera memorial stones
ThangadhSurendranagarMemorial stones and Chhatris
KanmerKutchTraditional memorial stones
SomnathGir SomnathHamirji Gohil memorial

Bhuchar Mori commemorates a specific historical battle, whereas the Sheera tradition of Jhalod includes different categories of community and ancestral memorials.

Prelims focus

  • Bhuchar Mori is situated near Dhrol in Jamnagar district.
  • The Battle of Bhuchar Mori took place in 1591 during Akbar's reign.
  • Prince Ajoji was associated with Nawanagar.
  • Sheera is a local term for memorial stones in Jhalod, Dahod.
  • Hamirji Gohil is remembered for the defence of Somnath.
  • Trap: Gujarat's memorial stones are not confined to Saurashtra and Kutch.

[Sources: Census of India, 1961, District Census Handbook: Jamnagar, Gazetteer of Place Names, Dhrol, p. 41; Ira Bhatnagar and Sushmita Sen, Documentation and Classification of the Paaliyas of Jhalod, Gujarat, 2024, section Paaliyas in Gujarat; Akashvani News, Somnath Swabhiman Parv Celebrates Thousand Year Legacy of Faith and Resilience, 9 January 2026. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Who were Vasant and Rajab?

Vasantrao Hegishte and Rajab Ali Lakhani were close friends and members of the Congress Seva Dal in Ahmedabad. They belonged to different religious communities but shared a commitment to social service and communal harmony.

Vasantrao came from a Hindu Maharashtrian family, while Rajab Ali belonged to a Muslim family. Their friendship acquired lasting significance because both sacrificed their lives while attempting to prevent communal violence.

The events of 1 July 1946

On 1 July 1946, communal disturbances occurred in Ahmedabad during the annual Jagannath Rath Yatra. Vasant and Rajab worked to protect people and prevent violence irrespective of religious identity. Both lost their lives in the Jamalpur area.

The incident occurred shortly before India's independence. Their sacrifice became a symbol of peaceful coexistence, friendship across religious boundaries and resistance to communal hatred.

Vasant–Rajab refers to 2 historical individuals remembered primarily as symbols of communal harmony. It is not the name of a religious festival, sporting event or artistic tradition.

Memorials associated with Vasant–Rajab

Vasant–Rajab Chowk

The locality around Khand ni Sheri in Jamalpur is associated with their sacrifice and is commemorated as Vasant–Rajab Chowk.

Bandhutva Smarak

The Bandhutva Smarak, also called the Vasant–Rajab Friendship Memorial, was inaugurated on 1 July 2015 at Gaekwad Haveli in Ahmedabad. An old watchtower within the haveli complex was adapted to house the memorial.

Gaekwad Haveli belongs to Ahmedabad's Maratha-period architectural heritage. Its association with Vasant–Rajab arose through the establishment of the modern memorial; the watchtower itself was not the original location of their deaths.

Commemoration and living heritage

The anniversary of their sacrifice, 1 July, has been observed by social organisations in Ahmedabad as Communal Harmony Day. Such commemorations keep the historical memory of Vasant–Rajab alive and communicate its significance to later generations.

The Vasant–Rajab tradition differs from the older Paliya tradition in its historical setting and commemorative form. Paliyas generally take the form of carved stone memorials, while Vasant–Rajab is remembered through public memorials, commemorative observances and civic narratives.

Prelims focus

  • Vasant: Vasantrao Hegishte.
  • Rajab: Rajab Ali Lakhani.
  • Both were members of the Congress Seva Dal.
  • They died on 1 July 1946 in Ahmedabad.
  • Bandhutva Smarak was inaugurated at Gaekwad Haveli on 1 July 2015.
  • Trap: Vasant–Rajab is principally associated with communal harmony, not a festival or the Quit India Movement.

[Sources: The Indian Express, For Image Makeover, Gujarat Crime Branch Opens Museum for Religious Harmony, 2 July 2015; The Times of India, Vasant-Rajab Heroism Will Be Memorialized at Gaekwad Haveli, 2014; The Indian Express, Communal Harmony Day on July 1, 28 June 2009; GPSC Prelims 2025, General Studies, Question 59, secondary reproduction on UnlockIAS, original Commission PDF unavailable. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Understanding folk deities

A folk deity, or Lok Devata, is a divine figure revered within popular religious traditions, often having a strong association with a particular community, locality, occupation or regional legend.

Folk worship may develop around mother goddesses, protective deities, legendary heroes and revered ancestors. The traditions are preserved through oral narratives, shrines, annual fairs, devotional songs and family customs.

Distinction between common religious terms

TermMeaning
Lok DevataA deity revered in popular or folk religious tradition
KuldevataA deity associated with a family, clan or lineage
KuldeviA female deity associated with a family, clan or lineage
Gram DevataA deity regarded as the guardian or patron of a village

These categories are not mutually exclusive. A goddess may be the Kuldevi of a royal family and simultaneously be revered as the patron deity of an entire region.

Ashapura Mata

Ashapura Mata is the traditional household goddess of the former Jadeja rulers of Kutch and is widely revered as the patron goddess of Kutch.

Her important shrine is located at Mata no Madh in Lakhpat taluka of Kutch district. Navratri is a particularly important period of pilgrimage to the shrine. Although Ashapura Mata has a strong historical association with the Jadeja dynasty, her devotees belong to different communities.

Khodiyar Mata

Khodiyar Mata, also known as Janbai or Khodal, is a widely revered folk goddess of Gujarat. Traditional accounts associate her origin with the Charan community. She is also worshipped as a family goddess by the Gohil Rajput dynasty.

An important Khodiyar Mata temple is situated at Rajpara near Bhavnagar, on the banks of Tataniya Wali Lake. The crocodile is her characteristic traditional vehicle, or Vahana.

The association of Khodiyar Mata with the Charan and Gohil traditions does not restrict her worship to those communities.

Bahuchara Mata

Bahuchara Mata is a form of the Mother Goddess. Her important shrine is located at Becharaji or Bahucharaji in Mehsana district.

She is revered by many families and has a particularly significant religious association with traditional hijra communities and other transgender devotees. This association is an important part of the shrine's cultural identity, but the goddess is worshipped by people from numerous social groups.

Randal Mata

Randal Mata, also known as Ranna Devi or Rannade, is traditionally regarded as the consort of Surya, the Sun God. Her worship is associated with childbirth, fertility, family welfare and the fulfilment of vows.

The Gujarati household tradition known as Randal na Lota involves the ritual representation of the goddess through a vessel. This is an example of a devotional custom in which worship does not necessarily require a permanent temple image.

Other important goddess associations

GoddessImportant associationPlace
Ashapura MataJadeja rulers and patron goddess of KutchMata no Madh, Kutch
Khodiyar MataCharan tradition and Gohil dynastyRajpara, Bhavnagar
Bahuchara MataMother Goddess and hijra devotional traditionsBecharaji, Mehsana
Randal MataSurya's consort and childbirth traditionsGujarati household worship
Amba MataShakti worshipAmbaji, Banaskantha
Kalika MataShakti worshipPavagadh, Panchmahal

Prelims focus

  • Kuldevi means the female deity of a family or lineage.
  • Ashapura Mata is associated with the Jadeja rulers of Kutch.
  • Khodiyar Mata is also known as Janbai; her traditional vehicle is the crocodile.
  • Bahuchara Mata Temple is at Becharaji in Mehsana.
  • Randal Mata is traditionally regarded as Surya's consort.
  • Trap: A deity's association with a particular community does not imply exclusive worship by that community.

[Sources: GCERT, Class 10, Social Science, Chapter 1, Heritage of India, section Gujarat's Cultural Heritage, Gujarati-medium edition consulted in place of the unavailable English compendium Volume 09; Government of Gujarat, Kachchh District, Mata Na Madh; Gujarat Tourism, Khodiyar Mandir and Bahuchar Mata Temple Becharaji; Shree Khodiyar Mata Mandir, Rajpara, temple information; A. M. T. Jackson, Folk Lore Notes, Vol. I: Gujarat, section on the worship of Randal Mata. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
